title: Chemical kinetics
note: A rate law, rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, must be found by experiment; the orders m and n need not match the coefficients. Integrated rate laws give straight-line plots: [A] vs t (zero order), ln[A] vs t (first order), 1/[A] vs t (second order). Rates rise with temperature because more collisions clear the activation energy, and catalysts open a lower-energy path.

read.title: How fast, and why
text: Kinetics asks how fast a reaction goes and what steps it takes. The rate is the change in concentration over time, and a rate law connects it to the concentrations of reactants: rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ. The exponents, called orders, can only be found by experiment. A common method compares initial rates: if doubling [A] doubles the rate, the reaction is first order in A; if it quadruples the rate, it is second order.

Integrated rate laws describe how concentration changes over time. For a first-order reaction, a plot of ln[A] against time is a straight line with slope −k, and the half-life, 0.693/k, does not depend on how much you start with. Radioactive decay follows this pattern.

Why does temperature matter so much? Molecules must collide with enough energy, the activation energy, and with the right orientation. Raising the temperature does not lower that barrier, but it gives a larger fraction of collisions enough energy to cross it. The Arrhenius equation, k = A·e^(−Ea/RT), puts this into numbers.

A catalyst offers a different route with a lower barrier. It speeds up both directions of a reaction, is regenerated at the end, and leaves ΔH unchanged. Enzymes are catalysts that make the chemistry of living cells fast enough to sustain life.
